name: SQL & Relational Database Architecture Track
description: Master relational database design, DDL schema creation, DML data manipulation, multi-table JOINs, subqueries, indexing, transactions, and enterprise analytics.
whatYouLearn: Execute DDL statements (CREATE TABLE, ALTER, DROP, FOREIGN KEY)
Master multi-table JOIN operations (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER)
Perform aggregate analytical queries with GROUP BY and HAVING
Optimize query performance with B-Tree Indexes and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Build an E-Commerce Analytics Relational Database

exercises.title: DDL Table Creation & Primary Keys (CREATE TABLE)
exercises.description: Create relational database tables with constraints and AUTO_INCREMENT primary keys.
exercises.theory: Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and modifies table structures. Primary keys uniquely identify rows.
exercises.objective: Create a users table with PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL constraints.
requirements: Create user_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT
Add NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraints to username and email
Set created_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
hints: VARCHAR(n) specifies maximum string length n
exercises.codeExample: CREATE TABLE items (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);

exercises.title: DML Data Insertion & Querying (INSERT INTO, SELECT)
exercises.description: Insert records and query table rows using column aliasing.
exercises.theory: Data Manipulation Language (DML) manages table row contents. SELECT projects columns and AS creates output aliases.
exercises.objective: Insert rows and query table data.
requirements: Insert two user rows with INSERT INTO
Select username and email with AS column aliases
hints: AS specifies display name aliases for query result columns
exercises.codeExample: INSERT INTO t (col) VALUES ('val'); SELECT col AS c FROM t;

exercises.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE Clause & Logical Operators
exercises.description: Filter rows using WHERE, AND, OR, NOT, and BETWEEN operators.
exercises.theory: WHERE clauses evaluate condition expressions to filter returned rows before aggregation.
exercises.objective: Query products priced between $20 and $100.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT product_name, price, category 
FROM products 
WHERE price BETWEEN 20.00 AND 100.00 
  AND is_active = TRUE 
ORDER BY price DESC;
requirements: Use WHERE with BETWEEN 20.00 AND 100.00
Add AND is_active = TRUE condition
Order results using ORDER BY price DESC
hints: BETWEEN is inclusive of start and end boundary values
exercises.codeExample: SELECT * FROM items WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50;

exercises.title: Pattern Matching & Sets (LIKE, IN, IS NULL)
exercises.description: Filter strings with wildcards (LIKE '%text%') and test set memberships (IN).
exercises.theory: LIKE matches string patterns (% represents multiple wildcard characters, _ represents single character). IN tests against a list of values.
exercises.objective: Find users with bytecode.io emails in specific departments.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT username, email, department 
FROM employees 
WHERE email LIKE '%@bytecode.io' 
  AND department IN ('Engineering', 'Product') 
  AND manager_id IS NOT NULL;
requirements: Use LIKE '%@bytecode.io'
Use IN ('Engineering', 'Product')
Use IS NOT NULL check
hints: Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead of = NULL
exercises.codeExample: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'a%' AND role IN ('admin', 'user');

exercises.title: Updating & Deleting Rows (UPDATE, DELETE, SAFE GUARDS)
exercises.description: Update existing records and delete rows with strict WHERE criteria.
exercises.theory: UPDATE modifies existing row values. DELETE removes matching rows. Always include WHERE clauses to prevent mutating all rows in a table.
exercises.objective: Update user roles and delete inactive accounts.
requirements: Execute UPDATE with SET and WHERE user_id = 42
Execute DELETE with double WHERE conditions
hints: Executing UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE modifies every single row in the table
exercises.codeExample: UPDATE users SET active = TRUE WHERE id = 1;

exercises.title: Foreign Keys & Relational Integrity (FOREIGN KEY)
exercises.description: Enforce referential integrity between tables using FOREIGN KEY constraints.
exercises.theory: Foreign keys link columns in child tables to primary keys in parent tables, preventing orphaned record creation.
exercises.objective: Build an orders table referencing users(user_id) with ON DELETE CASCADE.
exercises.initialCode: -- Create orders table with foreign key
exercises.solutionCode:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    total_amount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    order_date TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_orders_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) 
        REFERENCES users(user_id) 
        ON DELETE CASCADE
);
requirements: Define foreign key referencing users(user_id)
Include ON DELETE CASCADE clause
Use DECIMAL(10, 2) for currency amounts
hints: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes child orders when parent user row is deleted
exercises.codeExample: FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

exercises.title: Inner Joins (INNER JOIN)
exercises.description: Combine matching records from multiple tables using INNER JOIN.
exercises.theory: INNER JOIN returns rows only when there is a matching key value in both joined tables.
exercises.objective: Join users and orders tables on user_id.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    u.username,
    u.email,
    o.order_id,
    o.total_amount,
    o.order_date
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.total_amount > 50.00
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC;
requirements: Use table aliases u for users and o for orders
Join ON u.user_id = o.user_id
Filter total_amount > 50.00
hints: ON clause specifies key equality matching condition
exercises.codeExample: SELECT * FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id;

exercises.title: Outer Joins (LEFT JOIN & RIGHT JOIN)
exercises.description: Retrieve all parent records regardless of whether child matches exist using LEFT JOIN.
exercises.theory: LEFT JOIN returns all records from left table, along with matched records from right table (filling NULL for missing right matches).
exercises.objective: Find all users including users who have never placed an order.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    u.user_id,
    u.username,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0.00) AS total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username;
requirements: Use LEFT JOIN to include users without orders
Use COALESCE(SUM(...), 0.00) to replace NULL with 0.00
Group by user_id and username
hints: COALESCE returns first non-null argument
exercises.codeExample: SELECT u.name, o.id FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;

exercises.title: Aggregate Functions & Grouping (GROUP BY, SUM, AVG, COUNT)
exercises.description: Group table rows and calculate statistical summaries.
exercises.theory: GROUP BY summarizes rows by distinct column values. Aggregate functions include COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX().
exercises.objective: Calculate total order volume and average spend by department.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    department,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
    ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary,
    MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
requirements: Group by department column
Calculate COUNT(*), ROUND(AVG(salary), 2), and MAX(salary)
hints: Non-aggregated columns in SELECT must appear inside GROUP BY clause
exercises.codeExample: SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM items GROUP BY category;

exercises.title: Filtering Group Aggregates (HAVING Clause)
exercises.description: Filter aggregated group results using the HAVING clause.
exercises.theory: WHERE filters rows before grouping occurs. HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY computation finishes.
exercises.objective: Find departments with more than 5 employees and average salary > $80,000.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    department,
    COUNT(*) AS total_staff,
    ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(salary) > 80000.00;
requirements: Group by department
Filter using HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(salary) > 80000.00
hints: HAVING is used for aggregate conditions like SUM() > X, while WHERE is for individual row conditions
exercises.codeExample: SELECT cat, SUM(val) FROM t GROUP BY cat HAVING SUM(val) > 100;

exercises.title: Subqueries & Scalar Nested Queries
exercises.description: Write scalar subqueries inside WHERE and SELECT clauses.
exercises.theory: A subquery is a nested SELECT query enclosed in parentheses that returns values to an outer primary query.
exercises.objective: Find employees earning more than the company average salary.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    employee_id,
    first_name,
    last_name,
    salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) 
    FROM employees
)
ORDER BY salary DESC;
requirements: Write scalar subquery (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
Filter outer query WHERE salary > subquery
hints: Scalar subqueries return a single single-cell value
exercises.codeExample: SELECT * FROM t WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM t);

exercises.title: Correlated Subqueries & EXISTS Operator
exercises.description: Write correlated subqueries evaluated per candidate row using the EXISTS operator.
exercises.theory: Correlated subqueries reference columns from the outer query. EXISTS evaluates to TRUE if the inner subquery returns one or more rows.
exercises.objective: Find customers who placed at least one high-value order (> $500).
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    u.user_id,
    u.username,
    u.email
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM orders o 
    WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id 
      AND o.total_amount > 500.00
);
requirements: Use WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders ...)
Correlate inner subquery with outer table u.user_id
hints: EXISTS stops scanning subquery rows as soon as the first match is found
exercises.codeExample: SELECT * FROM u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM o WHERE o.u_id = u.id);

exercises.title: Common Table Expressions (WITH CTE)
exercises.description: Break complex queries into readable pipeline steps using WITH CTE statements.
exercises.theory: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) define named temporary result sets using the WITH keyword for modular multi-step query construction.
exercises.objective: Build a CTE calculating user spend metrics, then query high-tier users.
exercises.solutionCode:
WITH UserSpendCTE AS (
    SELECT 
        user_id,
        COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders,
        SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT 
    u.username,
    cte.total_orders,
    cte.total_spent
FROM UserSpendCTE cte
INNER JOIN users u ON cte.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE cte.total_spent > 1000.00
ORDER BY cte.total_spent DESC;
requirements: Define WITH UserSpendCTE AS (...)
Join CTE with users table in main query
Filter total_spent > 1000.00
hints: CTEs improve query readability compared to deeply nested subqueries
exercises.codeExample: WITH Summary AS (SELECT user_id, SUM(val) FROM t GROUP BY user_id) SELECT * FROM Summary;

exercises.title: Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK)
exercises.description: Compute row rankings and moving totals without collapsing rows using OVER(PARTITION BY).
exercises.theory: Window functions perform calculations across related row sets without collapsing table rows into single output summary rows.
exercises.objective: Rank top-earning employees within each department using DENSE_RANK().
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    department,
    employee_id,
    first_name,
    salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY department 
        ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS salary_rank
FROM employees;
requirements: Use DENSE_RANK() OVER (...)
Partition by department and order by salary DESC
hints: PARTITION BY splits window function calculations into department groups
exercises.codeExample: SELECT name, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat ORDER BY price DESC) FROM items;

exercises.title: Database Indexing & Query Optimization (CREATE INDEX)
exercises.description: Accelerate slow lookup queries by creating single and composite B-Tree indexes.
exercises.theory: Indexes create lookup trees on table columns to avoid expensive full table scans. Composite indexes optimize multi-column WHERE clauses.
exercises.objective: Create composite index on orders table for user_id and order_date.
requirements: Execute CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders (user_id, order_date DESC)
Inspect execution plan with EXPLAIN
hints: Put most selective columns first in composite index definitions
exercises.codeExample: CREATE INDEX idx_user ON users(email);

exercises.title: ACID Transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK)
exercises.description: Execute atomic database transactions guaranteeing all-or-nothing execution.
exercises.theory: Transactions preserve ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). COMMIT saves changes permanently; ROLLBACK cancels pending updates.
exercises.objective: Execute a safe money transfer transaction block.
requirements: Start transaction block with START TRANSACTION / BEGIN
Execute debit and credit UPDATE queries
Commit changes with COMMIT
hints: If any query inside transaction fails, call ROLLBACK to undo changes
exercises.codeExample: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE a SET bal = bal - 10; COMMIT;

exercises.title: Database Views (CREATE VIEW)
exercises.description: Encapsulate complex SQL queries into reusable virtual table views.
exercises.theory: Views are virtual stored queries that act like tables without duplicating underlying data storage.
exercises.objective: Create a UserSalesSummary view joining users and orders.
exercises.solutionCode:
CREATE VIEW vw_user_sales_summary AS
SELECT 
    u.user_id,
    u.username,
    u.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0.00) AS total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username, u.email;

-- Query view like a normal table
SELECT * FROM vw_user_sales_summary WHERE total_spent > 500.00;
requirements: Create view using CREATE VIEW vw_user_sales_summary AS ...
Query view using SELECT * FROM view_name
hints: Views simplify complex reporting queries across application services
exercises.codeExample: CREATE VIEW v_active AS SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = TRUE;

exercises.title: Database Triggers (BEFORE / AFTER INSERT)
exercises.description: Automate database audit logging using event triggers.
exercises.theory: Triggers automatically execute procedural SQL code when INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE events occur on a table.
exercises.objective: Build a trigger logging user deletion events into an audit log table.
exercises.solutionCode:
CREATE TABLE user_audit_log (
    log_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    deleted_user_id INT,
    deleted_username VARCHAR(50),
    deleted_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_after_user_delete
AFTER DELETE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO user_audit_log (deleted_user_id, deleted_username)
    VALUES (OLD.user_id, OLD.username);
END; //
DELIMITER ;
requirements: Create user_audit_log table
Create AFTER DELETE trigger referencing OLD.user_id and OLD.username
hints: OLD pseudo-record references deleted row values in DELETE triggers
exercises.codeExample: CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER DELETE ON users FOR EACH ROW BEGIN ... END;

exercises.title: Case Statements & Conditional Column Calculations
exercises.description: Perform conditional logic inside SELECT queries using CASE WHEN expressions.
exercises.theory: CASE WHEN evaluates boolean conditions inline to return specific values for calculated query result columns.
exercises.objective: Classify user spending tiers using CASE WHEN.
exercises.initialCode: -- Query user spend tiers with CASE WHEN
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT 
    username,
    total_spent,
    CASE 
        WHEN total_spent >= 1000.00 THEN 'VIP Tier'
        WHEN total_spent >= 250.00 THEN 'Gold Tier'
        ELSE 'Standard Tier'
    END AS customer_tier
FROM vw_user_sales_summary
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
requirements: Write CASE WHEN clause with multiple threshold conditions
Alias calculated column AS customer_tier
hints: CASE statements evaluate sequentially and return value for the first matching WHEN condition
exercises.codeExample: SELECT price, CASE WHEN price > 100 THEN 'High' ELSE 'Low' END AS tier FROM t;

exercises.title: Capstone Project: E-Commerce Analytics Database Architecture
exercises.description: Build an E-Commerce Analytics Database System featuring DDL Table Schemas, Foreign Keys, Indexing, CTE Analytics, and Customer Segmentation Views.
exercises.theory: This capstone project integrates relational database engineering: DDL table design, foreign key integrity, indexing, multi-table JOIN analytics, WITH CTEs, and database views.
exercises.objective: Engineer a complete Relational Database Analytics architecture.
exercises.solutionCode:
-- 1. DDL Schema Setup
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sales_orders (
    order_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    customer_id INT NOT NULL,
    amount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    order_date TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- 2. Indexing Optimization
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_customer_date ON sales_orders (customer_id, order_date);

-- 3. Analytics View with CTE
CREATE VIEW vw_customer_analytics AS
WITH CustomerAggregates AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders,
        SUM(amount) AS total_revenue
    FROM sales_orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    COALESCE(ca.total_orders, 0) AS total_orders,
    COALESCE(ca.total_revenue, 0.00) AS total_revenue,
    CASE 
        WHEN ca.total_revenue >= 1000 THEN 'Platinum'
        WHEN ca.total_revenue >= 500 THEN 'Gold'
        ELSE 'Standard'
    END AS segment
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN CustomerAggregates ca ON c.customer_id = ca.customer_id;

SELECT * FROM vw_customer_analytics;
requirements: Create customers and sales_orders tables with foreign key constraints
Create composite B-Tree index on sales_orders
Build vw_customer_analytics view using WITH CTE and CASE WHEN segmentation
hints: Combine DDL tables, foreign keys, CTE aggregates, and CASE WHEN customer segmentation
exercises.codeExample: CREATE VIEW v AS WITH c AS (...) SELECT * FROM c;
